h1: Olive Oil Fried Egg: The Spanish Method for Crisp Edges and a Soft Yolk
excerpt: A Spanish-style fried egg wants a pool of hot olive oil, not a film, and a spoon working the yolk while the white blisters at the edge. The method is short, but the oil quantity is where most home cooks fall short.
keyTakeaway: Use two to three tablespoons of oil for one egg, hot enough to bubble the instant the egg lands, and spoon it over the yolk instead of flipping. Salt the white once it firms, not the yolk. Extra virgin adds its own pepper and grass; a milder oil stays out of the way.

intro: A fried egg made in olive oil is not the same food as one made in butter or a splash of neutral oil. The white blisters and crisps at the edge, the yolk stays loose under a set surface, and the pan smells of the oil itself.
Most of that comes down to one thing people underdo at home: the amount of oil in the pan.

sections.heading: Why olive oil changes a fried egg

blocks.text: Butter shallow-fries an egg gently and browns as it goes; a neutral oil stays silent and does very little. Olive oil sits between the two — hot enough to blister the white properly, with a flavour of its own that a neutral oil never brings to the plate.
It is a shallow-fry, and the oil is doing real work, not just keeping the egg from sticking.

sections.heading: How much oil: a shallow pool, not a film

blocks.text: One egg wants two to three tablespoons of oil — enough that it pools around the white and rises partway up its edge, not a thin coating wiped across the pan. That is more than most home cooks pour, and it is the single biggest reason a homemade version falls flat.
A wider pan needs more oil to keep the same depth — judge by the pool, not the tablespoon.

sections.heading: Pan heat, then spooning oil over the yolk

blocks.text: The oil should shimmer and move like water before the egg goes in, and the white should bubble hard the moment it lands. A quiet pan gives a pale, rubbery edge instead of a crisp, lacy one — the step that separates a fried egg from a poached one.
Once the white is bubbling, tilt the pan and spoon the pooled oil over the yolk five or six times. This sets a thin skin on the yolk without cooking it through, so the egg never has to be flipped.

Salt the white once it has firmed at the edges, while it is still in the pan and can take the seasoning evenly. Leave the yolk unsalted until the egg is plated — salt sitting on a still-liquid yolk can toughen its surface before it ever reaches the table.

sections.heading: Extra virgin against a milder oil

blocks.text: Extra virgin carries its own pepper and grass into the egg, noticeable in the last of the pooled oil mopped up with bread. A milder, lighter oil fries cleaner, letting the egg taste mostly of itself and the salt.

items: **Extra virgin.** A visible flavour on the plate — good with plain bread or vegetables that can carry it.
**A milder oil.** Quiet and neutral, useful when the egg sits beside something already strongly flavoured.
**Either way**, keep the [six infused flavours](/products) for other dishes; their own character would compete with the yolk rather than sit under it.

blocks.text: Once the pan holds enough oil and it is hot enough, the frying itself takes under two minutes from the moment the egg goes in. This order keeps the white crisp at the edge and the yolk loose in the middle, without a flip.

items: Warm two to three tablespoons of oil over medium-high heat until it shimmers and moves freely.
Crack the egg into a cup first, then slide it into the oil close to the surface.
Let the white hit the oil hard — it should bubble and blister at the edges within seconds.
Salt the white once its edges have firmed.
Tilt the pan and spoon the pooled oil over the yolk five or six times.
Lift the egg out with a slotted spoon the moment the edges turn deep gold and lacy.
Drain briefly on the pan's edge and plate at once, while the yolk is still loose.

blocks.text: More oil than you think, hot enough to bubble on contact, spooned over the yolk instead of flipped, and salted on the white only. Extra virgin brings its own flavour; a milder oil stays quiet.

faqs.q: How much olive oil do I need to fry one egg?
faqs.a: More than a normal fried egg gets: two to three tablespoons, enough that the oil pools around the white and rises up its edge instead of lying flat as a thin film underneath it.

faqs.q: What pan temperature is right for an olive oil fried egg?
faqs.a: Medium-high, with the oil shimmering before the egg goes in. It should bubble hard around the white the instant it lands — a quiet pan gives a pale edge rather than a crisp one.

faqs.q: Why do you spoon oil over the yolk instead of flipping the egg?
faqs.a: Spooning hot oil over the top sets the yolk's surface gently while the underside keeps frying, so the centre stays loose. Flipping cooks the yolk through to its middle instead.

faqs.q: When should I salt an olive oil fried egg?
faqs.a: Salt the white once it has firmed at the edges, still in the pan. Leave the yolk unsalted until the egg is plated, since salt on a still-liquid yolk can toughen its surface.

faqs.q: Does extra virgin olive oil taste different from a milder oil when frying an egg?
faqs.a: Yes. Extra virgin carries its own pepper and grass into the dish, which some cooks want and others find too assertive for breakfast. A milder oil fries cleaner and lets the egg taste of itself.

faqs.q: Can I reuse the oil after frying an egg in it?
faqs.a: Strain it to remove any white or shell first. As general guidance, a shallow-fry oil like this is good for two or three uses with filtering, then it should be retired.

faqs.q: Is an olive oil fried egg the same as a Spanish-style fried egg?
faqs.a: Very close. Spain's huevos fritos use the same deep pool and basting, though some cooks push the edges further, to a deeper brown and proper crackle than most home versions reach.
